group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature
examples: How do beans climb up poles?

explain.say: Peas, grapes and passionflowers cannot hold themselves up, so they climb. Many use tendrils, thin curly shoots that search for something to grab.

faq.q: How does a tendril feel what it touches?
faq.a: Tendrils are very sensitive to touch. Cells on their surface respond to pressure, and in some plants a light touch lasting under a minute is enough to start them curling.

faq.q: Why do tendrils coil like springs?
faq.a: The coiled section acts like a spring. It pulls the plant up close to its support but can stretch, so wind does not snap the stem. Darwin noticed that each coil twists one way, then switches and twists the other way.
asks: Why do tendrils twist both ways?

faq.a: Climbing lets a plant reach sunlight without spending energy on a thick, strong stem of its own. It borrows the support of trees, fences and other plants.
asks: What is the point of climbing?

faq.a: Plants like beans and morning glories wind their whole stem around a support as it grows, sweeping in circles until they hit something. Each kind usually twines in the same direction.
Charles Darwin wrote a whole book on them, The Movements and Habits of Climbing Plants. He watched tendrils sweep in circles and coil when they touched something.
asks: What did Darwin learn about climbing plants?

facts: Charles Darwin first published his study of climbing plants in 1865 and expanded it into a book in 1875.
A coiled tendril twists one way along part of its length and the opposite way along the rest, with a switch point in between.
